text: Chapter 1 introduced the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as a source of technical risk categories. At the organizational level, it's structured as a continuous loop a governance program runs across a system's whole life, not a one-time document.

Govern sets the policies and accountability structures before any specific system is built. Map identifies a given system's intended use, stakeholders, and specific risks — this is where the threat model from the last lesson plugs in. Measure generates evidence about how the system actually behaves, including through red-teaming. Manage acts on what Measure found, prioritizing and tracking risk over the system's lifecycle. A program that only ever writes a policy and stops hasn't actually managed anything.

The EU AI Act is real, enacted regulation, not a hypothetical, and it's built as a risk pyramid. Unacceptable-risk practices, like social scoring by public authorities, are banned outright. High-risk systems — used in employment, credit scoring, or critical infrastructure — face the heaviest obligations: documented risk management, conformity assessments, and human oversight. Limited-risk systems like chatbots face transparency obligations, such as disclosing that users are talking to an AI. Minimal-risk systems, the large majority, face no additional obligations under the Act.

ISO/IEC 42001 is the published international standard for an AI management system — the AI-specific counterpart to how ISO/IEC 27001 standardizes information security. It gives organizations a certifiable structure: documented policies, defined roles, risk assessment, and continual improvement that an external auditor can actually assess. In practice, a cross-functional AI governance board — security, legal, data science, and often a responsible-AI role — reviews each system against all three: its EU AI Act risk tier, its NIST RMF evidence, and whether its documentation holds up against a certified management system.

That board review is exactly where the threat model and red-team findings from the last two lessons land. Next, you'll see why responsible AI and security aren't separate review tracks at all — a biased model and an insecure model are usually symptoms of the same governance gap.
